metadata.title: Bitcoin surges past $71,000 as Trump pushes Clarity Act

content.text:
President Donald Trump urged Congress on Thursday to pass cryptocurrency legislation, sending Bitcoin up more than 11% to above $71,000 and sparking a broad rally across digital assets.
CNBC reported Bitcoin changing hands at $71,880, while Barron's cited a slightly different figure of $71,732. Over that same stretch, Ethereum climbed 19% and XRP was up 15%. Bitcoin remains well below its all-time high of $126,198, set last October, and a 2026 peak of $94,820 reached in mid-January.
Trump and financial regulators made the case at a White House summit for Congress to pass the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act, which would place Bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies under commodity regulations rather than securities laws, according to Barron's. Among the executives in attendance were Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong, Intercontinental Exchange CEO Jeffrey Sprecher, Ripple CEO Brad Garlinghouse, and Robinhood Markets CEO Vlad Tenev.
Hyperliquid's token surged 26% after Trump announced that CFTC Chairman Mike Selig was engaged in efforts to bring the decentralized crypto exchange to the U.S.
Treasury yields also pulled back on Thursday after the U.S. Treasury announced plans to at least double its longer-term bond buyback program, a move that boosted the appeal of higher-risk assets such as Bitcoin. Trading volume in the iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF ran more than 4.5 times its 30-day average even before the Hyperliquid headlines, according to CNBC.
The crypto rally comes as the Clarity Act faces an uncertain path in the Senate. The Senate departed Washington without taking up the bill before its August recess, with Senate Majority Leader John Thune filing a cloture motion that sets up a procedural vote on September 15. That vote requires 60 votes to advance the bill; a failed result could effectively kill the legislation.
The bill has drawn opposition from Democrats who say it lacks sufficient anti-money laundering safeguards and strong enough ethics provisions, as well as resistance from parts of the banking sector. A separate sticking point — whether state attorneys general or the Justice Department should enforce the bill's ban on government officials operating crypto businesses — remains unresolved. When lawmakers return September 14, they will have only 14 working days before an October election recess.
